chapters.title: A Day at the Beach
chapters.summary: In this chapter: counting at the beach; chikoos, block sticks and ten strips; making 100 with ten strips; tens, ones and orange trays.

lessons.title: Counting at the Beach

activities.prompt: How can we count all the beach things in different ways?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways to Count at the Beach
activities.body: Counting at the beach can be done in different ways. Count each object one by one. You can also count shells, balloons, and bananas in bunches or groups. Children are encouraged to count in groups. Surbhi has collected seashells and wants to help make bracelets and necklaces. Her mother has made groups of shells for necklaces. Each shell necklace uses ten shells.
keyPoints: Objects can be counted one by one.
Objects can be counted in bunches or groups.
Each shell necklace uses ten shells.
activities.explanation: Groups make counting easier, and one-by-one counting also works.

activities.prompt: Surbhi has 9 seashells on the table. Count them one by one. How many seashells does she have?
steps: There are 9 seashells on the table.
Count every shell once.
Counting one by one gives 9 seashells.

gen.template: Surbhi has {shells} seashells on the table. Count them one by one. How many seashells does she have?

Count every shell once.
Counting one by one gives {answer} seashells.
gen.hint: Count each shell once.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: Surbhi has seashells for necklaces. Her mother makes groups of shells. How should Surbhi count them?
steps: Surbhi can count every shell one by one, because each shell is one object.
She can also count the shells in groups, because groups hold many shells.
Her mother makes groups for necklaces, so counting in groups fits the task.
Each necklace uses ten shells, so each necklace group needs ten shells.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Beach objects can be counted one by one.
activities.explanation: You can point to each object and count it.

activities.explanation: There are 3 groups with 5 balloons in each group. Multiply the number of groups by the number in each group. 3 x 5 = 15 balloons.

Multiply the number of groups by the number in each group.
3 x 5 = 15 balloons.
activities.hint: Count how many balloons are in each group.

activities.explanation: There are 20 seashells altogether. Each necklace group contains 10 shells. Counting in groups of 10 gives 2 groups. Dividing 20 by 10 gives 2 groups.
steps: There are 20 seashells altogether.
Each necklace group contains 10 shells.

activities.explanation: There are two groups with 3 shells and 4 shells. Add the number in each group: 3 + 4 = 7. The two groups contain 7 shells altogether.

The two groups contain 7 shells altogether.

activities.prompt: Each shell necklace uses ten shells. A child counts only the necklaces. Why is that not enough?
options: Ten shells in each necklace must be checked.
The number of necklaces is always ten.

This mistake confuses necklaces with shells.

why.Ten shells can make any number of neckla: This mistake thinks ten shells can make any number of necklaces.

activities.explanation: Counting necklaces alone cannot check that each one has ten shells.

lessons.title: Chikoos, Block Sticks and Ten Strips

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what happens when we count chikoos, blocks, and little units?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Groups of Ten
activities.body: Chikoos, block sticks and ten strips are in this lesson. Manoj helps his father sell chikoos. The chikoos are arranged in trays, and some are placed in trays of ten. One activity asks for objects that come in packs of ten. A block stick shows a number of blocks. A ten strip shows a number of units. Children complete a table. Grouping sticks or similar material helps develop number sense.
keyPoints: Some chikoos are placed in trays of ten.
Block sticks show blocks and ten strips show units.
Grouping materials helps develop number sense.
activities.explanation: You have learnt how groups can show numbers clearly.

activities.prompt: A block stick is shown with 8 blocks. How many blocks are on the block stick?
steps: The block stick shows 8 blocks.
Count every block once: 8 = 8.
The answer is 8 blocks.

gen.template: A block stick is shown with {n} blocks. How many blocks are on the block stick?
steps: The block stick shows {n} blocks.
Count every block once: {n} = {count}.
The answer is {answer} blocks.
gen.hint: Look at the blocks on the stick and count them once each.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.title: Build it with blocks

tasks.say: Make 100 using only ten strips.
tasks.when: th == 0 and hu == 0 and te == 10 and on == 0
tasks.then: Ten tens make one hundred.

tasks.say: Make 34.
tasks.when: th == 0 and hu == 0 and te == 3 and on == 4
tasks.then: 3 tens and 4 ones make 34.

tasks.say: Make 250.
tasks.when: th == 0 and hu == 2 and te == 5 and on == 0
tasks.then: 2 hundreds, 5 tens and no ones make 250.

tasks.say: Make 106 and notice the empty tens.
tasks.when: th == 0 and hu == 1 and te == 0 and on == 6
tasks.then: 1 hundred, no tens and 6 ones make 106.

tasks.say: Show 14 using one ten and four ones.
tasks.when: th == 0 and hu == 0 and te == 1 and on == 4
tasks.then: 14 ones can be grouped as 1 ten and 4 ones.

activities.takeaway: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred and 10 hundreds make 1 thousand.
activities.explanation: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred and 10 hundreds make 1 thousand.

lessons.title: Making 100 with Ten Strips

activities.prompt: Can we make exactly 100 using just ten strips?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Ten Strips Make 100
activities.body: Ten strips help us make 100. One example uses seven yellow strips and three red strips. It also has 70 yellow units and 30 red units. We can show the total with units or ten strips. Other combinations of ten strips can make a 100 units grid. A ten strip stands for ten units.
keyPoints: Seven yellow strips and three red strips make 100.
The example has 70 yellow units and 30 red units.
Units and ten strips can both show the total.
activities.explanation: Ten strips can show the total as 100 units.

activities.prompt: A child has 5 ten strips. How many units are on the ten strips altogether?
steps: Each ten strip has 10 units.
Multiply 5 strips by 10 units on each strip.
5 x 10 = 50 units, so the answer is 50 units.

gen.template: A child has {a} ten strips. How many units are on the ten strips altogether?
steps: Each ten strip has {strip_units} units.
Multiply {a} strips by {strip_units} units on each strip.
{a} x {strip_units} = {total_units} units, so the answer is {answer} units.
gen.hint: Remember that each ten strip has ten units.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

Writing with 0 and 1–9 began in India.

activities.prompt: Explain how the rule for a number greater than 50 differs from the rule for a number between 47 and 59.
activities.answer: A number greater than 50 must be above 50. A number between 47 and 59 must lie in that stated range. A number such as 59 can therefore meet both rules, while a number in the range below 50 does not.

A number can meet both rules.

activities.context: A learner has beads and blank cards on a ginladi. Counting the beads shows the numbers to write. Cards showing 38, 44, 58, 65, and 98 are placed on the ginladi. Blanks on the number strip are filled. The butterfly moves toward the pink flower. The honey bee moves toward the red flower and then the yellow flower. The squirrel jumps two steps backward, then five steps forward. The frog jumps two steps forward, then seven steps backward.
activities.prompt: One card on the ginladi is still blank. What should the learner do to complete it?
options: Count the beads and write their matching number on the card.
Choose a number without counting and write it on the card.
Leave the card blank because the beads do not need numbers.
Count the number cards instead of the beads and write that number.

why.Choose a number without counting and wri: A number chosen without counting may not match the beads.
why.Leave the card blank because the beads d: The activity says to write the beads' numbers on the cards.
why.Count the number cards instead of the be: The card must match the beads, not the number of cards.

activities.explanation: Counting the beads identifies the number that belongs on the card.

activities.context: A learner has beads and blank cards on a ginladi. Counting the beads shows the numbers to write. Cards showing 38, 44, 58, 65, and 98 are placed on the ginladi. The squirrel jumps two steps backward, then five steps forward. The frog jumps two steps forward, then seven steps backward.
activities.prompt: If the squirrel jumps five steps forward first and two steps backward afterward, where will it finish compared with its original route?
options: At the same finishing place as before.
Two steps behind its original finishing place.
Five steps behind its original finishing place.
Two steps ahead of its original finishing place.

why.Two steps behind its original finishing: This mistake counts only the backward jump and ignores the forward jump.
why.Five steps behind its original finishing: This mistake treats the forward jump as if it were backward.
why.Two steps ahead of its original finishin: This mistake adds the backward jump instead of subtracting it from the forward jump.

activities.explanation: The two jumps still combine to the same net movement.

activities.prompt: How does counting the beads help to fill the blanks on the number strip?
activities.answer: First, count the beads on the ginladi. Write the matching number on each blank card. Place the number cards showing 38, 44, 58, 65, and 98 on the ginladi. Then use the number strip and the cards to find and fill every blank with the correct number.
points: Counts the beads on the ginladi.
Writes the matching number on each blank card.
Places the number cards on the ginladi.
Uses the number strip and cards to fill the blanks.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Three ants are sitting on a number line, and 79 is shown on the number line. One ant is drawn on 65, and a sugar cube must also be drawn. In a guessing game, one child thinks of a number while the other children guess it. They can ask yes-or-no questions, including whether it is more than 50, whether its two digits are the same, and whether it is less than 20. They may ask at most 10 questions. An example guess is 30.
activities.prompt: The children have already asked ten questions in the guessing game. What should they do next?
options: End the questioning and make the best guess from the answers so far
Ask one more yes-or-no question
Continue asking as many questions as they wish
Ask ten more yes-or-no questions

why.Ask one more yes-or-no question: This breaks the limit on the number of questions.
why.Continue asking as many questions as the: This wrongly treats the question limit as unlimited.
why.Ask ten more yes-or-no questions: This wrongly allows another 10 questions after reaching the limit.

activities.explanation: This respects the limit of at most 10 questions.

why.Ask if the hidden number is less than 20: This also checks the size of the number, not its digits.
why.Ask if the hidden number equals 79: This checks one number instead of comparing the two digits.

activities.prompt: Explain how yes-or-no questions help the children guess the number and what the 10-question limit means.

Says to make a guess after the tenth answer

activities.answer: The sequence moves backward by 1 each time, so the next number after 8 is 7. The number just before 10 is 9, and the number just before 9 is 8. Each new place is one number smaller than the last.

activities.prompt: When do shadows appear, and what makes them disappear?

activities.title: Discover Togalu
activities.body: Nakul and his friends saw Togalu at a village fair. They were all fascinated by the shadow play. They wanted to make shadows too. They made different animal shadows. Puppetry is an art form practised in Karnataka. The puppets depict scenes from Indian epics. The role-play uses animal shadows. The children also create the animals’ sounds. You can try making shadows too.
keyPoints: Togalu was seen at a village fair.
The children made different animal shadows.
Puppetry shows scenes from Indian epics.
activities.explanation: You can explore shadows, animal sounds, and stories from Indian epics.

activities.prompt: At the village fair, 4 children each made 3 animal shadows. How many animal shadows did they make altogether?
steps: Each of the 4 children made 3 animal shadows.
There are 4 equal groups with 3 shadows in each group.
Multiplying the groups gives 12 = 12 animal shadows.

gen.template: At the village fair, {n} children each made {k} animal shadows. How many animal shadows did they make altogether?
steps: Each of the {n} children made {k} animal shadows.
There are {n} equal groups with {k} shadows in each group.
Multiplying the groups gives {total} = {answer} animal shadows.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: Nakul and his friends watch Togalu Gombeyaata at a village fair. They make animal shadows and animal sounds. Why does their role-play use both?
steps: The role-play uses shadows of different animals, because these shapes show the animal parts.
The children also create animal sounds, because the sounds add to the animal role-play.
The fair fascinated them, so they wanted to practise by making shadows too.
Therefore, their activity uses both animal shadows and sounds, and other children can try it too.

Create the animals' sounds but put the shadows aside.
Choose scenes from an Indian epic instead of using animal shadows.

activities.title: Lines in Yoga Poses
activities.body: Yoga poses can have standing lines, which are also called vertical lines. Some poses show vertical and slanting lines together. Other poses show curved lines or sleeping lines, also called horizontal lines. Children can try these poses and talk about the lines they notice. The teacher can help children practise and can tell them about Ashtanga Yoga.
keyPoints: Standing lines are called vertical lines.
Some poses have vertical and slanting lines.
Children can try poses and discuss the lines.

activities.title: Pull the thread

tasks.say: Now make a sleeping line.
tasks.then: A sleeping line lies flat: a horizontal line.

tasks.say: Make a slanting line.
tasks.then: Between standing and sleeping, a slanting line is still straight.

tasks.say: Bring your hands closer. What happens to the thread?
tasks.then: It droops into a curved line: it is not straight any more.

activities.takeaway: A tight thread is a straight line: standing, sleeping or slanting. A loose thread makes a curved line.
activities.explanation: A tight thread is a straight line: standing, sleeping or slanting. A loose thread makes a curved line.

activities.title: Folding Paper
activities.body: Folding paper in half makes a crease in the centre. Keeping it folded helps more creases appear. After folding, children can see different lines. Straight lines are traced with a red crayon, while slanting lines use a blue crayon. Children can also try to make curved lines.

chapters.title: Which Season is it?
chapters.summary: In this chapter: seasons and seasonal festivals; calendar fun; matching activities and time; a family trip.

lessons.title: Seasons and Seasonal Festivals

activities.prompt: Which fun festivals are connected to each season?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Five Seasons
activities.body: The year has five seasons. Spring brings cheer, blooming flowers and singing birds. Summer has a shining sun and long days. Autumn brings falling leaves and pleasant winds. Winter has snow from head to toe. Monsoon is another season. Autumn matches Dussehra and Sharad Purnima. Summer includes Guru Purnima and Buddha Purnima. Spring matches Gudi Padwa, Shivratri, Baisakhi and Holi. Monsoon matches Janmashtami, Raksha Bandhan and Independence day.
keyPoints: The year has five seasons.
Each season has its own special signs.
Different festivals are matched with the seasons.
activities.explanation: The seasons have signs, and festivals are matched with them.

activities.prompt: A child sees flowers blooming and birds singing. The child calls the season summer. How can we check the claim?
steps: Blooming flowers and singing birds show that spring has begun.
Cheer also begins with spring, so this sign agrees with them.
A shining sun and a long day describe summer, not these spring signs.
The child's claim is wrong, so the season should be spring.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Shining Summer
activities.prompt: Which season has a shining sun and a long day?
options: Spring
Summer
Autumn
Winter
activities.explanation: Summer has a shining sun and a long day. You matched the season correctly.

activities.title: Signs of Spring
activities.prompt: Spring begins with cheer, flowers blooming and birds singing.
activities.explanation: Yes. These are all signs of spring.

activities.prompt: Match each season to one festival from your book.
activities.explanation: These festivals are matched with the seasons in your book.

activities.explanation: Guru Purnima is matched with summer. Each other pair joins a festival with the wrong season.

options: Flowers and birds fit spring; sun and long day fit summer.

why.All signs fit summer because the sun and: The child sees summer signs but wrongly ignores the spring signs.
why.All signs fit autumn because falling lea: The child uses autumn signs that the park sign does not show.

Snow belongs to summer; pleasant winds belong to spring.

why.Snow belongs to autumn; pleasant winds b: The child swaps the autumn and winter signs.
why.Snow belongs to spring; pleasant winds b: The child wrongly gives snow to spring and winds to summer.
why.Snow belongs to summer; pleasant winds b: The child wrongly gives snow to summer and winds to spring.

activities.explanation: The child correctly separates winter's snow from autumn's pleasant winds.

why.Summer matches the leaves, winds, Dusseh: The child wrongly believes summer is matched with this autumn festival pair.

activities.explanation: Autumn matches the leaves, winds, Dussehra and Sharad purnima.

why.Move all cards to spring, because every: The child copies Holi's spring match to every festival.
why.Move all cards to autumn, because every: The child copies Dussehra's autumn match to every festival.

lessons.title: Matching Activities and Time

activities.prompt: How can we match activities with the time they take?

activities.title: Activities and Duration Choices
activities.body: Cooking is one activity to match with a duration. Summer vacation is another activity to match. Knitting a sweater is an activity. Growing a seed into a plant is another activity. Read each activity and look for a matching word.
keyPoints: Cooking and summer vacation match with a duration.
A change of season is an activity.
Hours and months are duration choices.
activities.explanation: Activities tell us what to match, while hours and months give duration choices.

activities.prompt: Cooking takes 4 hours. How many hours does the cooking take?

activities.prompt: Suppose the friend had spent 20 rupees more on rides. What would have happened?
options: The friend would still have had 8 rupees left.
The friend would have had 28 rupees left.
The friend would not have had enough money, because 42 and 20 make more than 50.
The friend would have had exactly 50 rupees to spend.

why.The friend would still have had 8 rupees: Mistake: thinks 20 more rupees spent changes nothing about the 8 left.
why.The friend would have had 28 rupees left: Mistake: adds the extra 20 to the 8 leftover instead of to the 42 spent.
why.The friend would have had exactly 50 rup: Mistake: confuses the money spent with the whole 50 rupees.
